new_statements.rule_in_words: Ilongot, like every language in Paz's first-hand 29-language sample, is treated as having phonemic (lexically contrastive) stress, marked with an acute; her Ilongot citations show stress on either the penult or the final syllable, i.e. the familiar Philippine two-syllable window with unpredictable placement. Dedicated Ilongot descriptions (M. Rosaldo 1968 in Reid 1971; M. Rosaldo 1980) phonemicize the same suprasegmental as vowel length rather than stress and give no placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ilongot specifically; the statement is a blanket one for all 29 languages. Paz sec. 3.6.5 discusses stress only for the reconstructions (marked where found in the closest cognate, else by majority).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (single words elicited via a Tagalog-based list from one informant); word-level lexical stress; no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Paz 1981's Ilongot data ('Igt') were elicited from one speaker (Lucas Pesigian) of Lipuga, Dupax del Sur, Nueva Vizcaya; Reid 1971 / M. Rosaldo describe the Kakidugen (Kakiduge:n) dialect. All are ilon1239 (no Glottolog sub-dialects). Note the analytic split: Paz writes contrastive stress (buwán vs. ʔápo), whereas M. Rosaldo 1968/1980 and Zorc's data sheets write the same suprasegmental as phonemic vowel length (qabi:ka, dɨ:num) — the usual Philippine 'accent = penult length' equivalence, not a factual disagreement.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3.3 lists Ilongot (Igt, Lipuga, Dupax del Sur, informant Lucas Pesigian) among the 29 first-hand languages and states 'All languages have phonemic stress, /ˊ/' (printed p.23). Ilongot forms in the appendix dictionary are cited with contrastive stress on penult or ultima (e.g. Igt ʔápo, bádu, gákap, díguy vs. buwán, lumót, suntók, ʔabúk).
